title: Kinetic Proofreading Activation Times Beyond the Weibull Limit
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, submitted to Physical Biology
summary: T cells can detect a few foreign peptide-major histocompatibility complexes (pMHCs) among a far larger number of self pMHCs. Kinetic proofreading explains this discrimination: a receptor that has bound its ligand must complete nKP signaling steps, each at rate kp, before it activates, and dissociation at any step resets its progress. When many receptors are engaged at once, the time to the first activation has been approximated by a Weibull law taken from the short-time limit of this process. The Weibull law is convenient, but it does not contain the dissociation rate koff, even though koff is what proofreading uses to tell ligands apart. Using the exact first- passage law of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain together with stochastic simulations, we show that the relative error of the Weibull law is set by a single dimensionless number {\Lambda}, the Weibull-predicted activation time measured in units of nKP + 1 bound-state lifetimes. For {\Lambda} < 1 the first receptor to activate does so before its ligand has ever dissociated, and the Weibull law holds. As {\Lambda} grows, activation relies increasingly on repeated unbinding and rebinding. The true activation time then exceeds the Weibull prediction by up to 2900-fold on our parameter grid, and the effective Weibull shape falls to one, so activation becomes memoryless instead of timer-like. We derive a closed form that keeps koff by treating the successful pass through the proofreading chain separately from the time lost to failed attempts. It matches exact medians to within 2% in 19 of 25 parameter sets, with a worst case of about 6%, and reproduces the loss of timer-like behavior. Because {\Lambda} is computed from the Weibull prediction itself, it shows in advance how far that formula can be trusted; where it cannot, the new expression requires only a one-dimensional root find.

AI.tldr: The study shows that the Weibull law fails to predict T cell activation times when ligands dissociate frequently, and proposes a new closed-form expression that incorporates the dissociation rate to accurately model activation times and the loss of timer-like behavior.
AI.motivation: The Weibull law, used to approximate the time to the first T cell activation, fails to include the dissociation rate (koff), which is critical for kinetic proofreading and ligand discrimination.
AI.method: The authors employ the exact first-passage law of a continuous-time Markov chain combined with stochastic simulations to evaluate the Weibull law's error and derive a new closed-form expression.
AI.result: The error in the Weibull law increases as Λ grows, with activation times exceeding Weibull predictions by up to 2900-fold; the new closed-form model matches exact medians within 2-6% accuracy and reproduces the loss of timer-like behavior.
AI.conclusion: The Weibull law is a reliable approximation for T cell activation time only when Λ < 1, but it fails significantly as Λ increases because it ignores the dissociation rate (koff). A new closed-form expression that incorporates koff and accounts for multiple unbinding/rebinding events is proposed, providing highly accurate predictions of the median activation time and the transition from timer-like to memoryless behavior.

title: TAPESTRY: an interactive resource for exploring tumor-enriched splice junctions in pediatric brain tumors
summary: TAPESTRY (this https URL) is a database and web application for exploring recurrent tumor-enriched splice junctions (TEJs) in pediatric brain tumors, cancers that carry few protein-coding mutations and therefore few mutation-derived neoantigens. However, TEJs represent a much larger source of neoantigens as potential therapeutic targets in these tumors. TAPESTRY catalogs 45,430 recurrent TEJs across 19 histologies, identified in 1,962 RNA-seq specimens (including 1,272 independent primary tumors) from the Pediatric Brain Tumor Atlas and compared to four normal brain reference cohorts comprising adult, pediatric, developmental and cell-type-resolved tissue. Each junction is classified as tumor-specific or oncofetal; annotated for splice-event type, coding consequence, novelty relative to GENCODE v39 and overlap with Pfam and UniProt protein domains; and scored for recurrence within each histology. Users can search by gene or splicing event and filter results by histology, junction class, and annotation. Users can also generate gene-level expression heatmaps across cohorts, junction-level expression boxplots, and transcript and exon diagrams, and download all tables and figures. A documented REST API supports programmatic access, and all source code is openly available. By making tumor-selective and developmentally reactivated splicing events searchable and interpretable, TAPESTRY supports the prioritization of splice-derived targets for antibody-based, cell-based and vaccine immunotherapies in pediatric brain and central nervous system tumors.

AI.tldr: TAPESTRY is a specialized database and web application designed to identify and catalog recurrent tumor-enriched splice junctions (TEJs) in pediatric brain tumors to facilitate the discovery of novel neoantigens for immunotherapy.
AI.motivation: Pediatric brain tumors often lack protein-coding mutations, resulting in few mutation-derived neoantigens. TEJs offer a significantly larger reservoir of potential therapeutic targets.
AI.method: The researchers analyzed 1,962 RNA-seq specimens (including 1,272 primary tumors) against four normal brain reference cohorts. They identified 45,430 recurrent TEJs across 19 histologies, classifying them by specificity (tumor-specific vs. oncofetal), coding consequence, and protein domain overlap.
AI.result: A comprehensive, searchable platform with built-in visualization tools (heatmaps, boxplots, transcript diagrams) and a documented REST API for programmatic data access.
AI.conclusion: TAPESTRY provides a scalable resource to prioritize splice-derived neoantigens for antibody, cell-based, and vaccine-based immunotherapies in pediatric CNS tumors.

title: Phase-based Edge Coupling: Modeling Overlapping Functional Architectures and High-Order Edge-to-Edge Interactions in EEG Networks
summary: Network neuroscience has traditionally relied on node-centric approaches, which are inherently limited in capturing the brain's overlapping functional architectures and higher-order edge-to-edge interactions. The emerging edge-centric paradigm addresses this gap by shifting the analytical unit from nodes to edges. However, while edge-centric models have been established for DTI and fMRI, comparable EEG methodologies have yet to be developed. In this study, we proposed a Phase-based Edge-centric Coupling (PEC) algorithm for EEG network modelling, where edge time series are derived from instantaneous phase differences of EEG signals and edge-to-edge coupling is quantified via normalized inner product. Simulation tests demonstrated the robustness of PEC algorithm, achieving high accuracy (<10% relative error) in coupling estimation and discriminative capacity (AUROC>0.7) against spurious this http URL provided sufficient data length(>=16 cycles), PEC outperformed traditional Phase Node-centric Coupling (PNC) in both individual identifiability and cognitive-state identifiability, enabling superior characterization of stable individual neural signatures and dynamic task-dependent functional configurations. Furthermore, unlike PNC's hard-partitioned modularity, PEC captured highly overlapping yet functionally specialized modular structures and connector hubs, aligning with task-engaged cognitive processes. Applied to dyadic interactions, PEC identified distinct cross-brain modules encoding symmetric and asymmetric neural coordination. These findings establish PEC as a valid and powerful tool for EEG network modelling, providing new insights into the brain's complex, multifunctional organization at both intra-brain and inter-brain networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new EEG modeling method called **Phase-based Edge-centric Coupling (PEC)**, which shifts focus from brain nodes to the interactions between edges to better capture complex neural architectures.
AI.motivation: Traditional node-centric EEG analysis fails to capture overlapping functional structures and higher-order edge-to-edge interactions. While edge-centric models exist for fMRI/DTI, they are missing for EEG.
AI.method: The PEC algorithm derives edge time series from instantaneous phase differences and quantifies edge-to-edge coupling using a normalized inner product.
AI.result: 1. **Robustness:** High accuracy (<10% error) and good discriminative capacity (AUROC > 0.7). 2. **Superiority:** Outperforms node-centric models (PNC) in individual and cognitive-state identifiability. 3. **Complexity:** Captures overlapping modular structures and connector hubs rather than rigid partitions. 4. **Application:** Successfully applied to dyadic (inter-brain) interactions to identify symmetric/asymmetric neural coordination.
AI.conclusion: PEC is a powerful tool for EEG modeling, providing deeper insights into both intra-brain and inter-brain network organizations.

title: Dynamics of a Harvested Predator-Prey Model with a Generalized Holling Type~III Response Capturing Group Defense
summary: We investigate a predator-prey model with constant prey harvesting and a generalized Holling type III functional response, focusing on the biological and dynamical consequences of allowing the parameter $b$ to be negative. In this regime, predation efficiency declines at high prey densities, potentially reflecting group defense. This change permits an additional coexistence equilibrium and introduces new bifurcation mechanisms affecting population persistence. We establish the existence of a codimension-three Bogdanov--Takens bifurcation, derive a codimension-three nilpotent-saddle unfolding, and investigate a codimension-two generalized Hopf bifurcation and the emergence of multiple limit cycles. Our analysis show that moderate harvesting weakens the protection conferred by high prey abundance; excessive harvesting leaves too few prey to sustain predator growth; and low harvesting preserves strong group defense, requiring high predator density for population persistence.

AI.tldr: A study of a predator-prey model with constant prey harvesting and a generalized Holling type III response, specifically examining the effects of negative parameter $b$ which represents group defense.
AI.motivation: To investigate the biological and dynamical consequences of a negative parameter $b$ in a predator-prey model, which represents a scenario where predation efficiency declines at high prey densities due to group defense.
AI.method: Mathematical analysis of a predator-prey model with constant prey harvesting and generalized Holling type III functional response, including bifurcation analysis (Bogdanov–Takens, nilpotent-saddle unfolding, and generalized Hopf bifurcation).
AI.result: Discovery of an additional coexistence equilibrium and new bifurcation mechanisms, including the emergence of multiple limit cycles and specific population persistence thresholds related to harvesting levels.
AI.conclusion: Harvesting levels significantly impact population dynamics: moderate harvesting weakens group defense, excessive harvesting leads to population decline, and low harvesting maintains strong group defense.

title: From Heterogeneity to Function: Enhanced Modular Dynamic Range in Hierarchical Brain Networks
summary: Hierarchical and modular organization defines brain architecture, yet how it supports flexible computation and functional specialization remains unclear. Although dynamic range is a hallmark of efficient information processing, its distribution across modules and hierarchical levels remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that hierarchical-modular networks naturally generate heterogeneous modular dynamics and firing rates, extending regimes of critical-like dynamics with enhanced intrinsic timescales, reflecting critical slowing down, and diverse scaling exponents without fine-tuning near criticality. Intrinsic timescales increase across hierarchical levels, while their dispersion within levels emerges only when connectivity profiles and firing rates are heterogeneous. We introduce modular dynamic range to quantify how individual modules respond to external inputs and show that heterogeneity enhances both global and module-specific sensitivity, with modular intrinsic timescales increasing with dynamic range. Local stimulation reduces dynamic range in homogeneous networks but enhances it in heterogeneous networks relative to global stimulation. Moreover, selectively stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes both global and modular dynamic range, revealing a principle of functional specialization. In heterogeneous networks, modular dynamic range is more variable and increases even in unstimulated modules, demonstrating distributed computational benefits beyond directly stimulated regions. Together, these findings establish heterogeneity as a mechanism through which hierarchical-modular networks sustain critical-like dynamics, generate hierarchical timescales, and distribute computational sensitivity, providing a basis for functional specialization without fine-tuning to criticality.

AI.tldr: Heterogeneity in brain-like hierarchical networks enables complex, multi-scale information processing and functional specialization by sustaining critical-like dynamics and maximizing dynamic range across modules.
AI.motivation: To understand how the brain's hierarchical and modular architecture supports flexible computation and functional specialization, specifically focusing on how dynamic range and information processing efficiency are distributed across the network.
AI.method: The researchers utilized computational modeling of hierarchical-modular networks to analyze the distribution of dynamic range, intrinsic timescales, and scaling exponents across different hierarchical levels and modules.
AI.result:
Key findings include:
- **Critical-like Dynamics:** Heterogeneity allows networks to sustain diverse scaling exponents and extended timescales without fine-tuning.
- **Hierarchical Timescales:** Intrinsic timescales increase as one moves up hierarchical levels.
- **Modular Dynamic Range (MDR):** A new metric introduced to quantify module-specific sensitivity to inputs. Heterogeneity enhances both global and modular sensitivity.
- **Functional Specialization:** Stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes dynamic range, suggesting these levels play a crucial role in information distribution.
- **Distributed Benefits:** In heterogeneous networks, even unstimulated modules show increased dynamic range, indicating distributed computational advantages.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that heterogeneity in connectivity and firing rates is a fundamental mechanism that enables hierarchical-modular brain networks to achieve efficient computation and functional specialization without the need for precise fine-tuning to criticality.

title: Stochastic predator-prey compartment model with cyclic and non-cyclic transition pathways and mortality
summary: We study variants of a stochastic SEIRS-SEID compartmental model incorporating presymptomatic infectiousness and disease-related mortality, with independent compartmental sojourn times drawn from arbitrary distributions, in particular Weibull distributions. We consider a large population of agents that occupy the states (compartments) S (susceptible to infection), E (exposed: infected but asymptomatic during the latency period and already infectious, including diseases with presymptomatic infections), I (infected and infectious, with symptoms), R (recovered, immune, and non-infectious), or D (dead). We consider (i) cyclic transmission pathways, where compartmental sojourn times are finite and immunity is temporary, and (ii) non-cyclic pathways, where immunity is permanent. In the absence of mortality, cyclic transmission pathways support an endemic equilibrium above the spreading threshold which is either globally stable or oscillatory (Hopf) unstable, whereas for non-cyclic pathways a stationary disease-free state is emerging. From a stochastic perspective, we elucidate the connection between compartmental sojourn-time distributions and the appearance of fractional operators in the evolution equations: fat-tailed compartment waiting-time distributions necessarily lead to fractional derivatives. For cyclic transition pathways we obtain an explicit expression for the expected number of infection cycles that an agent survives. Our model is validated by a combined Monte Carlo -- Runge -- Kutta simulation scheme and random-walk simulations on Barabasi-Albert networks. It has cross-disciplinary applications beyond epidemiology, including wildfire spreading, certain classes of chemical reactions, population dynamics, finance, economics, and biology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a generalized stochastic SEIRS-SEID compartmental model that uses arbitrary sojourn-time distributions (specifically Weibull) to account for presymptomatic infectiousness and mortality.
AI.motivation: Traditional models often assume exponential sojourn times (Markovian). This study addresses the need for more realistic, non-exponential waiting times and their impact on disease dynamics.
AI.method: The authors use stochastic modeling, Monte Carlo-Runge-Kutta simulations, and random-walk simulations on Barabasi-Albert networks to analyze cyclic (temporary immunity) and non-cyclic (permanent immunity) pathways.
AI.result: 1. In cyclic pathways, the system reaches an endemic equilibrium that is either globally stable or exhibits Hopf instability. 2. Fat-tailed distributions in waiting times lead to the emergence of fractional derivatives in evolution equations. 3. The model provides an explicit expression for the expected number of infection cycles survived by an agent.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a robust framework for understanding complex transition dynamics and is applicable to various fields including epidemiology, wildfire spreading, finance, and population biology.

title: Estimation of the Cyclopean Eye from Binocular Free Visual Explorations
summary: Binocular video-oculography records separate signals for each eye, yet human visual processing and oculomotor control operate relative to a single, virtual cyclopean eye. This study addresses the estimation of the cyclopean eye during binocular free visual exploration, a target-free paradigm widely used for the screening of neurological disorders. Using eye-tracking data collected at 1 kHz from 113 participants across three cohorts (patients with Parkinson's Disease, age-matched healthy controls, and young controls), we compare two different methods: one based on an Independent Component Analysis and another based on Factor Analysis. The extracted cyclopean signals were evaluated on their ability to preserve clinically critical fixation and saccadic events using both velocity-threshold and pixel-dispersion event detectors, and were validated against references via Dynamic Time Warping. Results suggest that the technique based on Factor Analysis guarantees full identifiability across all subjects and achieves low alignment errors, performing comparably to the traditional Version Signal (point-wise mean) while dynamically adapting to inter-eye asymmetry. Furthermore, the second factor in this technique was empirically null across all fitted models, confirming that a single latent factor fully accounts for the shared binocular gaze dynamics. These findings establish Factor Analysis as an identifiable framework for estimating the cyclopean eye in target-free visual exploration protocols.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates methods to estimate a single 'cyclopean eye' signal from binocular eye-tracking data during free visual exploration, comparing Independent Component Analysis (ICA) against Factor Analysis (FA).
AI.motivation: Human visual processing uses a single virtual viewpoint, but binocular eye-trackers record two separate signals. Standard methods (like the point-wise mean) may fail to account for inter-eye asymmetries, which is critical for clinical neurological screening.
AI.method:
- **Dataset:** 1 kHz binocular eye-tracking data from 113 participants (Parkinson’s patients, age-matched controls, and young controls).
- **Comparison:** ICA vs. Factor Analysis (FA).
- **Evaluation Metrics:** Preservation of fixation/saccade events (velocity-threshold & pixel-dispersion) and alignment accuracy via Dynamic Time Warping (DTW).
AI.result:
- **Superiority of FA:** Factor Analysis provides full identifiability and low alignment error.
- **Dimensionality:** The second factor was empirically null in all models, proving that a single latent factor effectively captures shared binocular dynamics.
- **Performance:** FA performs comparably to the traditional 'Version Signal' (mean) but offers better dynamic adaptation to asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: Factor Analysis is a robust and identifiable framework for estimating cyclopean eye signals, making it suitable for clinical protocols in neurological disorder screening.

title: Computational De Novo Design of Miniprotein Candidate Neutralizers Targeting the IL-23 Cytokine Subunit p19
comment: Accepted as a short paper at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM 2026)
summary: Interleukin-23 (IL-23) drives T-helper-17 inflammation underlying inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis; anti-p19 antibodies are clinically effective but large, costly, and injectable. De novo miniproteins are an attractive alternative, yet published designs target the IL-23 receptor; the IL-23 cytokine itself has not been addressed. A further obstacle is that the standard confidence score (ipTM) tracks construct length rather than interface quality. We computationally design miniprotein binders against the IL-23R-binding face of p19 (PDB 3DUH) and score every design with ipSAE, a length-robust interface metric derived from AlphaFold-initial-guess predicted aligned error. A conventional RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN/ColabFold pipeline yields no reliable predicted interface across 972 designs (best ipSAE 0.30), and a scoring artifact, in which single-sequence ColabFold under-rates binder pLDDT by approximately 56 points, explains an earlier misleading "binders do not fold" signal. An interface-optimized hallucination method (BindCraft), scored identically, yields 42 of 50 designs above ipSAE 0.60 (best 0.804). An AlphaFold-independent geometric check reproduces the conventional failure: no top-ranked conventional design reaches the buried area or interface hydrogen-bond count of the weakest lead. Five all-alpha-helical leads (72-104 residues) collectively engage all six targeted hotspots; two dock within the intact p40/p19 heterodimer and all show favorable Rosetta energetics. A p40-alone counter-screen returns ipSAE 0.00 for all five, indicating no spurious p40 interface. To our knowledge, these are the first computationally proposed de novo miniprotein candidates designed to occlude the IL-23R-binding face of IL-23 p19. All results require experimental validation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first computational design of de novo miniproteins aimed at neutralizing the IL-23 cytokine (p19 subunit) by blocking its receptor-binding face.
AI.motivation: Current anti-p19 therapies (antibodies) are large, expensive, and injectable. Miniproteins offer a smaller, more cost-effective alternative, but existing designs focus on the receptor rather than the cytokine itself.
AI.method: The authors utilized 'BindCraft' (an interface-optimized hallucination method) to design binders against the p19 subunit (PDB 3DUH). They introduced **ipSAE**, a length-robust interface metric, to overcome the flaws of standard ipTM scores.
AI.result: The conventional RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN pipeline failed to produce reliable binders. In contrast, BindCraft produced high-quality leads (best ipSAE 0.804). Five alpha-helical leads (72-104 residues) successfully targeted all six hotspots and showed specificity against the p40 subunit.
AI.conclusion: The study successfully demonstrates that specialized interface-optimized design methods can overcome the limitations of standard pipelines for cytokine neutralization. Experimental validation is the required next step.

title: Shared clones make random cell halves look reproducible in pooled screens
comment: 48 pages, 7 figures; includes Supplementary Information. Code and result files: this https URL
summary: Single-cell perturbation screens are used to train and evaluate models that predict perturbation effects, and model scores are judged against how reproducible the measured effects are. Reproducibility is usually judged by splitting each perturbation's cells into two random halves. This assumes that the halves are independent replicates. In pooled screens such as Perturb-seq, however, the cells carrying a guide RNA descend from a limited number of transduced cells, so two random halves contain the same clones: pseudoreplication whose unit is not marked in the data. Using perturbations that should have no effect as controls, we compared random halves with independent replicates from separate transductions, and tested directly with halves that differ only in their clones. In a genome-scale screen of primary T cells, null perturbations agreed between random halves almost always and between independent replicates only half the time, the rate expected from noise alone; measuring more cells did not remove this agreement. Splitting the cells into halves that share no clone, by the T-cell receptor constant region or by a clone barcode, largely removed the excess agreement. Its size equals the share of expression differences set by clones divided by the effective number of clones per perturbation; across 16 screens it was largest in T cells transferred into mice and in a genome-scale primary T-cell screen, one to two orders of magnitude smaller in cell lines, and smallest in non-dividing neurons. Shared clones inflate benchmark ceilings and reliability labels, and when a model's input and its scoring answer come from one transduction, published models that predict perturbation effects in a new cell state appear better than a baseline that ignores the perturbation; against cells from another transduction, most fall below it. Reproducibility should be judged across separate transductions.

AI.tldr: Pseudoreplication in single-cell perturbation screens (like Perturb-seq) occurs because random cell splits often contain the same clones, leading to inflated reproducibility scores. To avoid biased model evaluation, benchmarks should be judged across separate transductions rather than random halves of the same transduction.
AI.motivation: Current reproducibility benchmarks for single-cell perturbation models often use random splits of cells from a single transduction, which incorrectly assume independence and ignore the presence of shared clones (pseudoreplication).
AI.method: The study compared random cell splits with independent replicates from separate transductions and analyzed splits that differ by clones (using T-cell receptor constant regions or clone barcodes) across 16 different screens, including T-cell and neuronal data.
AI.result: Random halves show high artificial agreement due to shared clones, whereas independent replicates show much lower agreement (expected from noise). Models evaluated on random splits appear superior to baselines, but perform poorly when evaluated against separate transductions.
AI.conclusion: To ensure reliable model evaluation, reproducibility in single-cell perturbation screens should be judged across independent biological replicates (separate transductions) rather than random cell splits from a single pool.

title: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
summary: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable to the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens, and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features -- directions that act like leading, spatially coherent Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a ``Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical applied to both model classes. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens . We also introduce of a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a theoretical framework for the 'Jacobian lens' (J-lens), explaining why it detects certain features in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Previous empirical work showed J-lens identifies 'working memory-like' directions, but the underlying mechanistic reason for this detection remained unknown.
AI.method: The authors develop a mathematical theory proving that J-lens preferentially identifies 'coherent features'—specifically, directions acting as leading Lyapunov modes that amplify across layers and maintain consistency across context.
AI.result: The theory was validated using a Bayes filter and a toy transformer (HMM-based tasks), where task-driven changes in feature coherence matched J-lens responses. They also introduced $\omega$-J-lenses to analyze different temporal scales.
AI.conclusion: The J-lens is mathematically biased toward detecting spatially coherent, amplifying directions, providing a theoretical basis for its empirical success in interpretability.

title: Virtual Placebo: a scoping review of control conditions in randomized controlled trials of psychological immersive virtual reality interventions
summary: Research on immersive virtual reality (IVR) as a therapeutic tool is growing rapidly, with randomized controlled trials (RCTs) now commonplace. Yet the control conditions in many of these studies that claim strong specific IVR effects vary from usual care to active immersive experiences, making it difficult to draw clinically meaningful conclusions. We conducted a scoping review of recent literature on psychological IVR interventions to assess the main forms of control conditions used and their relations to study outcomes. In this paper, we make the case that most of the recent RCTs studying the effects of specific IVR interventions compare active immersive VR to usual care with no multimedia component. This can lead to strong yet potentially misleading study outcomes and can potentially inflate the IVR interventions' effect. Namely, the lack of an appropriate immersive control condition may risk misattributing general effects of VR devices to the specific content of the intervention. In this review, we discuss the implications of these design choices and propose strategies for including a suitable "virtual placebo" condition to improve the methodological rigor and interpretability of results.

AI.tldr: A scoping review revealing that IVR research often lacks immersive control conditions, leading to potentially inflated effect sizes and a need for 'virtual placebo' designs.
AI.motivation: The inconsistency and inadequacy of control conditions in IVR studies (comparing active VR to mere usual care) may lead to inflated effect sizes and misattribution of device effects to specific intervention content.
AI.method: A scoping review of recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on psychological immersive virtual reality (IVR) interventions to assess control condition types and their impact on outcomes.
AI.result: Most recent IVR RCTs use control conditions without any multimedia component, which risks misinterpreting general effects of VR hardware as specific therapeutic effects of the intervention.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that current IVR research lacks methodological rigor due to inappropriate control conditions, and they propose using 'virtual placebo' conditions to better isolate the specific therapeutic effects of IVR content.

title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
summary: Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

AI.tldr: Researchers decomposed two popular annual Earth embeddings and demonstrated that they encode meaningful ecological features like fire, forest clearing, and crop types, validated across six continents.
AI.motivation: While annual Earth embeddings are increasingly used for ecological monitoring and carbon accounting, the semantic meaning of their learned vectors remains unestablished and opaque.
AI.method: The study performed a decomposition of two widely used embedding products to extract and interpret individual ecological features, validating them against independent reference data.
AI.result: The decomposition successfully recovered concepts such as abrupt canopy loss, fire severity (distinguishing wildfire from prescribed fire), and crop types, with performance varying slightly between the two products.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes that Earth embeddings contain interpretable ecological features that can be used for monitoring land-use changes and disturbances.

title: What Transfers Across Protein Pockets? Experience Reuse in Molecular Optimization for Agentic Structure-Based Drug Design
summary: LLM agents optimize a ligand in a protein pocket by editing it step by step and docking each edit. Recent agents first spend extra dockings probing the complex with controlled edits; guidance induced from these probes is reported to help more than the chemical knowledge the model already carries. The probes are then discarded with the instance that produced them, so the obvious next step is to keep them in an experience base, letting a new pocket inherit what earlier ones already paid for. Such a base is read through a \emph{key}: the record properties under which past edits are pooled and a new one is looked up. Using the full log of one such run over the CrossDocked2020 test-set pockets, we ask whether its keys recur on a pocket the base has never seen and still separate improving from worsening edits. \crchange{Using} the contacts at the site being edited, the action, and the round as \crchange{a} key, the base separates them sharply. Within our analysis, this separation is largely explained by how much the edit changed the molecule's size, the action, and the round, none of which describes the target. That is not because the target is irrelevant: naming it outright separates them several times more sharply. For a pocket absent from the base, transfer must rely on a description rather than its identity. Among the exact-match descriptions we evaluate, the more specific ones rarely recur, whereas the coarser ones provide little separation; the signals that do transfer primarily describe the edit and the molecule it produced rather than the target. Under the representations and lookup scheme studied here, an experience base may be more useful for prioritizing an agent's own proposals for docking than for directly prescribing what to build.

AI.tldr: An experience base based on current lookup schemes is better at helping an agent **evaluate its own proposals** (prioritizing docking) rather than **directly prescribing new structures** for unknown targets.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents spend computational resources on 'probing' edits that are discarded after use. The authors propose leveraging these probes in a shared memory to allow new tasks to benefit from previously 'paid-for' chemical insights.
AI.method: The authors evaluate an experience base composed of past docking trials. They test different 'keys' (descriptors) to retrieve past experiences, ranging from specific target identities to coarse structural descriptions, and analyze their ability to distinguish between successful and unsuccessful edits.
AI.result: 1. **Identity vs. Description:** Using the specific target identity is the most effective way to separate good from bad edits, but this fails for unseen pockets. 2. **Transferability Gap:** Coarse descriptions of the target (to allow for transfer) provide poor separation, while highly specific descriptions rarely recur. 3. **Source of Signal:** The predictive power in the current setup stems more from the properties of the *edit* and the *molecule* (size, action, round) rather than the properties of the *target*.
AI.conclusion: The paper investigates whether an 'experience base' (a memory of past ligand-protein edits) can facilitate knowledge transfer in LLM-driven drug design when encountering unseen protein pockets.

title: Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells
summary: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence, rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware, that trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QP2I), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. Thereby, QP2I enables to study contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes all-optically and label-free. It provides both structural and functional readouts at frame rates that are sufficient to temporally resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. While conventional fluorescent labels bleach out over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring, QP2I provides similar established structural readouts, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length, as well as previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, as a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity. QP2I thus enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast.

AI.tldr: QP2I is a single-shot, video-rate computational imaging framework that combines quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging using a standard DIC microscope and a polarization camera, enabling label-free, long-term monitoring of both structural and functional dynamics in live cells.
AI.motivation: Standard quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is blind to molecular order (anisotropy), while existing methods to capture birefringence often require slow multi-frame scanning or specialized interferometric hardware, which limits speed and complexity.
AI.method: A computational framework called QP2I that utilizes a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope equipped with a polarization camera, employing a globally regularized phase reconstruction and per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction.
AI.result: The system successfully provides quantitative phase and anisotropic retardance information at video rates, validated on simulations, static targets, muscle tissue, and living cardiomyocytes, allowing for real-time monitoring of sarcomere length and photoelasticity.
AI.conclusion: QP2I enables long-term, label-free, and quantitative interrogation of dynamic cellular processes, providing both structural and functional readouts without the drawbacks of fluorescent labeling.

title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators
summary: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **ZENO** (Zakai Equation Neural Operator), a physics-informed machine learning framework designed to approximate unnormalized filtering distributions in nonlinear stochastic systems using operator learning.
AI.motivation: Solving the Zakai equation (an SPDE governing filtering distributions) is analytically impossible and numerically intractable in high dimensions, which hinders state inference and parameter learning in scientific machine learning.
AI.method:
1. **ZENO Architecture**: Uses a neural operator trained via a physics-informed loss based on the Zakai equation to approximate the unnormalized posterior distribution. 
2. **EM Framework**: Integrates the ZENO-inferred distribution into an Expectation-Maximization loop for joint state inference and SDE parameter learning.
AI.result:
1. **Simulation**: Successfully recovered parameters and posteriors for complex systems (Double-Well, Van der Pol, and Lorenz). 
2. **Biological Application**: Successfully recovered locomotion limit cycles from *C. elegans* whole-brain imaging data.
AI.conclusion: ZENO provides a novel bridge between operator theory and nonlinear filtering, offering a scalable way to handle high-dimensional latent SDE inference.

title: A Central Limit Theorem for the Driver Site Frequency Spectrum
summary: We consider a supercritical two-type continuous-time linear birth-death process with mutation and selection, in which wild-type individuals give rise to mutant offspring with a larger net-growth rate. We previously had obtained first-order law of large number results for the driver site frequency spectrum. We return to obtain a second-order central limit theorem, in which we show stable convergence of a scaling of the deviation of the SFS from its first-order limit. We provide a central limit theorem at both large detection times and sizes. Then, we apply these results to obtain confidence intervals for a class of consistent estimators for the fitness advance.

AI.tldr: Extends previous first-order LLN results for driver site frequency spectrum (SFS) in supercritical two-type birth-death processes to include a second-order central limit theorem (CLT) for both large detection times and population sizes.
AI.motivation: To move beyond first-order law of large numbers (LLN) results and provide second-order asymptotic distributions (CLT) for the driver SFS to enable confidence interval estimation for fitness advance.
AI.method: Mathematical analysis of a supercritical two-type continuous-time linear birth-death process with mutation and selection, focusing on the scaling of the deviation of the SFS from its first-order limit.
AI.result: Established a second-order central limit theorem (CLT) for the SFS at large detection times and sizes, and applied it to construct confidence intervals for consistent estimators of fitness advance.
AI.conclusion: The second-order CLT provides a robust framework for quantifying the uncertainty in fitness advance estimators in the context of driver SFS.
